title: The storehouse at Sultanpur
hook: weighing out grain as a storekeeper, he reaches thirteen, tera, which also means yours, and keeps saying it

segments.voice: Yesterday: sacha sauda, the true bargain, twenty rupees turned into a meal. Your line was the best bargain. Who did you feed? Day twenty-seven.

Remember Bebe Nanaki, who made room for her brother in the town of Sultanpur? Here's what happened when he got there. Her husband, Jai Ram, found him a steady, respectable job, the kind his father had hoped for. The local governor, Daulat Khan Lodi, needed someone honest to run the government storehouse, where grain collected as taxes was kept and handed out as wages and supplies. So the young man who'd come home empty-handed from the market was put in charge of the grain. Tradition says he was good at it, and honest. He had a family of his own by now, and for a while it looked as if Mehta Kalu's son had finally settled down. Then came the day he started counting.
screen: `A STEADY JOB IN SULTANPUR.` → `THE GOVERNOR'S STOREHOUSE.` → `THEN HE STARTED COUNTING.`

segments.voice: The storehouse was called the modikhana, and a storekeeper measured out grain the old way: a scoop, a scale, counting out loud as each measure went into a customer's bag. One, two, three. In Punjabi: ik, do, tin. The story says one day Nanak was measuring out grain, counting as usual, up through ten, eleven, twelve. And then he reached thirteen. In Punjabi, thirteen is terah. Said aloud, it sounds just like tera, the Punjabi word for yours. As in: yours, God. All of it, yours. And he stopped counting. He just kept saying it. Tera. Tera. Tera. Scoop after scoop went into the bag, and every one was thirteen, every one was yours. It sounds like a man losing his mind at work. But look at what it says. Everything he was handing out, the grain, the scale, his own hands, the job, none of it was really his. It all belonged to God. So what was there to count? Someone, of course, complained to the governor that the storekeeper was giving the grain away. The accounts were checked. And the story says every grain was accounted for, and some tellings say there was even a surplus. In Sultanpur today there's a gurdwara where tradition says the storehouse stood, and weights said to be the ones he used are kept there. Here's the heart of it. Tera isn't a trick with numbers. It's a way of holding everything you have with open hands. My money, my house, my time become yours, lent to me for a while. And a person who really believes that tends to measure generously.
screen: `THE MODIKHANA — THE GRAIN STORE.` · `IK, DO, TIN... UP TO THIRTEEN.` · `TERA — THIRTEEN, AND YOURS.` · `THE ACCOUNTS CAME OUT RIGHT.` · then, large: `TERA, TERA, ALL YOURS.`

segments.voice: Let's count to thirteen together, slowly, one number per breath. Breathe in, and on the way out think one. Then two. Then three. Keep going, all the way to twelve. And when you reach thirteen, let it become tera, yours, and let everything you're holding today belong to something larger for a moment. Then just keep breathing, tera on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Modikhana. The government storehouse at Sultanpur, where Nanak weighed out grain and counted to tera: thirteen, and yours.
Your line: tera, tera, all yours. Today, when you hand something over, a payment, a meal, your time, think tera as you do it. Day twenty-seven.

screen: `DAY 27 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE DAYS IN THE RIVER.`

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the tera story as a sakhi of Guru Nanak's years in Sultanpur Lodhi, and pilgrims visit the gurdwara there where tradition says the storehouse stood.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: tera, yours. said aloud, it sounds like the word for thirteen.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man who lost count.
what it means: holding everything with open hands: the grain, the job, the hands themselves all belong to God.
what a scholar hears: the pun depends on Punjabi: tera (thirteen) and tera (yours) sound alike. Sultanpur Lodhi was a seat of the Lodi governor Daulat Khan.

notes: In Punjabi, thirteen is 'terah' (spellings vary) and 'yours' is 'tera' (ਤੇਰਾ); the pun depends on their sounding alike. The original game gives ਤੇਰਾ (yours). A Keeper should confirm the spelling note.
Gurdwara Hatt Sahib and the preserved weights (vatte): stated as 'tradition says'; confirm.
Marriage (to Mata Sulakhni) mentioned only as 'he married, started a family'; confirm placement in the Sultanpur years.
Surplus in the audit is in some tellings; confirm.

Editor review: fixed the pun (thirteen is terah, which sounds like tera, yours; the teach, myth and match had said they were one word); 'the most respectable job' and 'by all accounts' softened; 'he married' in Sultanpur removed (tradition places the marriage earlier).
